title: EV Range Radius Map: See the Range Ring
description: Visualise an electric car's usable range as a ring on the map with the EV Range Radius Map — one-way versus out-and-back, honestly drawn. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a 240-mile rated range draws a 240-mile one-way ring — but the out-and-back ring, the one a day trip actually lives in, is 120 miles in radius.
quick_answer: The EV Range Radius Map draws a vehicle's range as a ring around a point so trip planning starts from geography instead of a brochure number. Enter the range and see the one-way reach — remembering that a trip that must come home lives in half that ring.

Rated range 240 mi: one-way ring area π × 240² ≈ 180,956 mi² of map; out-and-back ring (r = 120) ≈ 45,239 mi². Coming home quarters the playground — the single most useful picture in EV trip planning.

Plan a cold trip at 70% of rated range — a planning allowance, not a measurement — and a 240-mile car becomes a 168-mile one-way ring, 84 miles out-and-back. The map redraws instantly; the disappointment happens indoors.

faq: Does the ring account for terrain and weather?
No — and it says so. Hills, cold, headwinds and motorway speeds all shrink real range. Treat the ring as the ceiling and plan inside it with a margin you choose.
Is a radius the same as driving distance?
No. The ring is straight-line reach; roads wind. A destination at 100 straight-line miles can be 130 road miles — check finalists by road before the trip.
Can I use this for service-area planning?
For EV fleets, as the geographic screen — yes. Depot rings show candidate coverage; charging locations then decide what is actually servable.
Are map measurements legal survey measurements?
Irrelevant here — a range ring is a planning sketch, not a boundary. Nothing legal hangs on it, which is part of its charm.
Why plan at half range for a return trip?
Because the battery must fund the journey home. Half is the geometry of out-and-back with zero margin; prudent planners use less than half.
One-way relocation trips?
Then the full ring is the honest one — a house move or a one-way rental drop can spend the whole range in one direction.
Does charging en route change the picture?
Completely — a charger at the ring's edge extends the day by another ring. This tool draws one ring at a time; chain them mentally along your route.
Should I plan to the ring's edge?
No — the edge assumes a full battery, still air and no detours. Experienced EV drivers plan arrivals with a buffer; the ring is the map of the possible, not the advisable.
Why is the ring a circle at all?
Because it is a first sketch. Real reach follows roads and chargers, which is why this page insists on its own limits and links the road tools.
Does speed change the ring?
Highway speeds cost range against rated figures, so a motorway day wants a smaller planning ring than a city day in the same car.
